**Pick PostgreSQL, with a `jsonb` column for the varied attributes.** You get the document flexibility where you need it and relational guarantees everywhere else.

```sql
CREATE TABLE products (
  id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  sku         text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name        text NOT NULL,
  category_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES categories(id),
  price_cents integer NOT NULL CHECK (price_cents >= 0),
  attributes  jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'
);
CREATE INDEX ON products USING gin (attributes jsonb_path_ops);
```

| Concern | PostgreSQL + `jsonb` | MongoDB |
|---|---|---|
| Varied attributes | `jsonb` column, GIN-indexed, queried with `@>` | Native; documents are the model |
| Fixed fields (SKU, price, category) | Typed columns, `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`, `CHECK`, foreign keys | Optional JSON Schema validation; no foreign keys |
| Related data (inventory, orders, pricing) | Joins and multi-table transactions are routine | `$lookup` and multi-document transactions work but are clumsier and slower |
| Ad hoc attribute queries | One GIN index covers containment on any key; range queries on a specific attribute need an expression index | Per-field or wildcard indexes; slightly nicer query syntax for nested data |
| Attribute updates | Rewrites the whole row; fine for a read-heavy catalogue | In-place field updates; better for very write-heavy documents |
| Horizontal scale | Single primary plus read replicas; sharding needs Citus or similar | Built-in sharding |
| Search and facets | Built-in full-text search; facet counts are hand-written SQL | Good facet aggregation, best with Atlas Search |

**Why Postgres wins here**
- A catalogue is never only the catalogue. Prices, stock, orders and categories are relational, and you will want joins and transactions across them.
- Only part of each product varies. The core fields are the same for every product and benefit from real constraints.
- It scales far enough: a read-heavy catalogue of millions of products fits comfortably on one node with replicas.

**When I would pick MongoDB instead**
- The catalogue is a standalone service with no joins to other data, and products are deeply nested documents read and written whole.
- You expect write volume or data size that requires sharding from the start.
- The team already runs MongoDB in production and has no Postgres experience.

If none of those apply, Postgres is the lower-risk choice.
